additions.text: The chocolate shop
chocolate maker
It is a chocolate shop. It smells very good. There is white, dark and milk chocolate. Greta works here.
Hi, I am Greta. Do you like chocolate?
Greta lets you taste three chocolates. Which one do you want?
The white chocolate, please.
Greta says: “It is very sweet. Children love it!”
The dark chocolate.
Greta says: “It is my favourite. It is a little bitter.”
The milk chocolate.
Greta says: “It is the most popular. How many do you want?”
Greta asks: “Is it a present?” She puts the chocolate in a red box. Who is it for?
Do you like chocolate?
Yes, I like it a lot. / Not much.
White, dark or milk?
When do you eat chocolate?
Do you like sweet things?
Yes, I like them. / I prefer salty things.
What is your favourite dessert?
Do you make desserts?
Who do you buy presents for?
For my mother / my partner / my friends.
What do you give them?
Do you like getting presents?
Is it cold in your city?
Yes, it is very cold. / No, it is hot.
What do you drink when it is cold?
Do you like the cold?
chocolate
sweet
bitter
the present
the box

Mitre Street, in the centre of Bariloche, has many chocolate shops. Greta comes from a family that arrived from Switzerland many years ago. In the window there is “chocolate en rama”, bonbons and alfajores.
My grandfather started with a small kitchen at home. Now the shop has three floors. Upstairs we make the chocolate and downstairs we sell it. Do you want to see how we make it?
You have money for one thing only. What do you buy?
A big box of “chocolate en rama”.
Greta explains it breaks easily and gives you a special bag for the trip.
Six alfajores to share.
Greta adds one more as a gift. “Always one more for the road.”
A one-hour class in the kitchen.
You put on an apron and make your own bonbons. They are not perfect, but they are yours.
The power goes out in the whole street. The chocolate in the kitchen starts to harden. Greta asks for your help. What do you do?
What typical food is there in your city?
In my city there is… / It is famous for…
Do you like it?
Where do you buy it?
Does your family come from another country?
Yes, my grandparents come from… / No, they are all from here.
What customs do they have?
Do you speak another language at home?
Can you cook something sweet?
Yes, I can make… / No, I can only eat.
Who taught you?
Who do you cook for?
What do you buy as a souvenir of a trip?
I always buy… / I don’t buy anything.
What is your favourite souvenir?
Where do you keep it?
the shop window
the bonbon
the apron
the souvenir
to share

It is high season and the chocolate shop is full of tourists and school groups on their graduation trip. Greta has been working since seven in the morning. A boy from one of the groups breaks a two-kilo chocolate figure.

Every year it is the same: thousands of fifteen- and sixteen-year-olds arrive, happy and without sleep. I love them, really, but that figure was a Saint Bernard that took me three days to make. Did you go on a trip like that with your school?
The boy is very nervous and has no money. The group coordinator is nowhere to be found. What do you advise Greta?
Call the travel company so they pay.
The company pays, but it takes two months. Greta sighs and keeps the invoice.
Have the boy help in the shop for an afternoon.
The boy works four hours, learns to make bonbons and in the end wants to come back next year.
Use the pieces to sell broken chocolate cheaper.
The tourists buy all the pieces in half an hour. Greta earns more than with the whole figure.
That night, the whole group comes back to the shop with a sign: “Sorry, Greta.” Each of them buys something.
Did you go on a school trip?
Yes, we went to… / No, we never went on a trip.
What do you remember from that trip?
Did you do anything forbidden?
Have you ever broken something expensive?
Yes, once I broke… / No, I am very careful.
What happened afterwards?
Did you have to pay?
What place in your country fills up with tourists?
In summer / winter, … fills up with…
Is it good for the people there?
Do you go in high season?
Have you ever worked with the public?
Yes, I worked in… / No, never.
Who was the most difficult customer?
Did you like it?
high season
graduation trip
to break
the invoice
the piece

An international chain wants to buy Greta’s family chocolate shop. It offers a lot of money and promises to keep the name, but wants to change the recipe for a cheaper one and move production to a factory in Buenos Aires.

My brother wants to sell. He says we are tired, that the business gets harder every year and that with that money we could live in peace. He is right about everything. But if they change the recipe, it is no longer our chocolate, it is just our surname on a box. What would you do?
Greta has to give an answer on Monday. What do you recommend?
Sell, but on condition that they keep the recipe.
The chain accepts it in the contract, but only for five years. After that, nobody knows.
Don’t sell and look for a smaller local partner.
A local hotel partners with them. They earn less, but the kitchen stays above the shop.
Sell everything and open something new and small under her own name.
Greta opens a ten-metre workshop. The queue of customers reaches the corner.
In an old box, Greta finds her grandfather’s recipe notebook. The original recipe is not the one they use today: it was already changed thirty years ago, without anyone noticing.
Would you sell a family business for a lot of money?
Yes, if… / No, because…
What condition would you set?
What would your family think?
What product from your country has lost quality over the years?
Before, … was better, now…
Why do you think it happened?
Do you still buy it?
Is it important that a tradition never changes?
I think so / not, because…
Can you give an example?
What tradition would you change?
Do you prefer small shops or big chains?
I prefer… because…
Where did you last buy something?
Would you pay more for local products?
the chain (of shops)
the business partner
the recipe
the surname
to notice
The lake harbour
boat captain
It is a big blue lake. There are mountains with snow. There is a white boat. Don Aníbal is the captain.
Good morning. I am Aníbal. Are you coming on the boat?
The boat goes to an island. Where do you sit?
Outside, to see the lake.
Aníbal says: “It is cold. Put on a jacket!”
Inside, near the window.
Aníbal says: “Good idea. There is hot coffee.”
With the captain, please.
Aníbal says: “Sure! Come. Here is the wheel.”
There are birds around the boat. Aníbal gives you bread. “Feed them!” What do you do?
Do you like boats?
Yes, I like them. / No, I get seasick.
Are there boats in your city?
Can you swim?
Is there a lake near your home?
Yes, there is a lake. / No, there is a river / the sea.
What is it called?
Do you go often?
What colour are the mountains in winter?
They are white. / They are green.
Do you like snow?
Is there snow in your country?
Do you like birds?
Yes, a lot. / Not much.
Do you have pets?
What is your favourite animal?
the lake
the boat
the island
snow
the jacket (Argentina)

Lake Nahuel Huapi is huge and the water is very cold, even in summer. From the harbour, boats leave for Victoria Island and the arrayán forest, trees with cinnamon-coloured trunks. Don Aníbal has been driving boats here for forty years.
This lake changes its mood like a person. In the morning it is calm, in the afternoon there is wind and waves. Today the day is perfect. Is it your first time in Patagonia?
There are three excursions today. Which do you choose?
The arrayán forest.
You walk along a wooden path among orange trees. It looks like a fairy tale.
Victoria Island, with a long walk.
You walk for three hours. You see ancient paintings on the rocks and a white-sand beach.
A short trip round the lake and back.
Aníbal tells you stories about the lake and shows you where a very rare bird lives.
Suddenly the wind starts and the boat rocks a lot. A woman gets scared. What do you do?
Do you prefer the mountains or the beach?
Where do you go on holiday?
What do you do there?
Do you swim in cold water?
Yes, I love it. / No, never!
Where do you swim?
How long can you stay in?
What do you like doing when it is sunny?
When it is sunny, I like…
And when it rains?
With whom?
Does anything scare you when travelling?
Planes / boats… scare me. / Nothing.
What do you do to stay calm?
Has it always been like that?
the harbour
the wave
the wind
the path
the forest

It is the last trip of the day and night is falling. Don Aníbal tells the legend of Nahuelito, a huge creature that, according to some locals, lives at the bottom of the lake. Many people laugh, but there are blurry photos from the eighties.

I didn’t believe in Nahuelito. One winter afternoon, in ’92, I saw a long shadow beside the boat, bigger than the boat itself. I told my wife and she laughed for three days straight. Do you believe in these things?
A passenger says he sees something moving in the water. Everyone looks. What do you do?
I take a photo quickly.
The photo comes out blurry, like all of them. Now you too have your Nahuelito photo.
I ask Aníbal to stop the boat.
Aníbal turns off the engine. Total silence. Only the water can be heard. Nobody breathes.
I laugh: it is surely a log.
Aníbal smiles: “That is exactly what I said in ’92.”
When they reach the harbour, a little boy asks Aníbal if Nahuelito is bad. Aníbal answers: “No. He is shy, like you.”
Is there a legend in your country?
Yes, they say that… / I don’t know any.
Who told it to you?
Do people believe it?
Have you ever seen something strange?
Yes, once I saw… / No, never.
Where were you?
Did you tell anyone?
What stories did people tell you as a child?
My grandmother / my father used to tell me…
Did they scare you?
Do you tell them now?
Do you like watching the sunset?
Yes, especially in… / I don’t pay attention to it.
What is the most beautiful sunset you have seen?
Who were you with?
the legend
the shadow
blurry
to get dark
the little boy (Argentina)

An investment group wants to build a private pier and a luxury hotel on a bay of the lake that is public today. There would be work for a hundred people, but locals could no longer swim or fish there. Don Aníbal has to speak at the neighbourhood meeting tonight.

My grandson needs work and that hotel would give him a job. But my father taught me to swim in that bay, and his father taught him. If we close it, today’s kids will only see the lake from the road. I don’t know what to say tonight. What would you say?
Aníbal has five minutes to speak. What do you suggest?
Support the hotel, but demand that the beach stays public.
The investors accept a twenty-metre public strip. Some locals call him a traitor; others, sensible.
Oppose it and propose the hotel somewhere else.
The meeting lasts four hours. In the end, the town council asks for a study of other sites.
Tell his personal story and not say how to vote.
The room goes quiet. Several young people change their minds, and some old ones too.
After the meeting, Aníbal’s grandson confesses that he already signed a contract with the hotel last week.
Should natural places always be public?
Are there exceptions?
What happens in your country?
What is more important: jobs or the landscape?
It depends on… / For me, …
Can you have both?
What example do you know?
Have you ever taken part in a neighbourhood meeting?
Yes, once we discussed… / No, I never went.
How did it end?
Did you speak?
What place from your childhood has changed a lot?
Before it was… and now it is…
For better or worse?
Do you go back sometimes?
the pier
the bay
to demand
the town council
sensible
Cerro Catedral
ski instructor
It is a mountain with a lot of snow. There are people with skis. It is very cold. Lola is the ski teacher.
Hi! I am Lola. Can you ski?
Lola has three activities. What do you want to do?
I want to ski.
Lola says: “Very good! Slowly at first.”
I want to go up on the chairlift.
Lola says: “Up there, there is a very nice view.”
I want to drink a hot chocolate.
Lola says: “Me too! Let’s go to the café.”
You fall in the snow! Lola laughs and gives you her hand. What do you say?
Do you like winter?
Yes, I like it. / No, I prefer summer.
Why?
What do you do in winter?
Do you do any sport?
Yes, I play… / No, I don’t do sport.
When?
What clothes do you wear when it is cold?
I wear a jacket / hat / gloves.
Do you have a scarf?
What colour is it?
Do you like mountains?
Yes, a lot. / I prefer the sea.
Are there mountains in your country?
Which is the highest?
the mountain
to ski
the chairlift
the cold
to fall

Cerro Catedral is one of the largest ski resorts in South America. In July, families arrive from all over the country and from Brazil. Lola teaches beginners from nine in the morning until four in the afternoon.
My students today are a family from São Paulo. They had never seen snow. The kids are happy and the parents are scared to death. Will you help me translate a little?
The dad doesn’t want to go down the slope. What do you tell him?
“Relax, we go very slowly.”
The dad takes fifteen minutes to go down a hundred-metre slope. At the end, he claps.
“Look at your kids: they can do it!”
The dad looks at the kids, breathes and goes down. He falls twice, but laughs.
“You can wait in the café.”
The dad happily accepts. From the window, he takes photos of the whole family.
The youngest girl of the family gets lost in the crowd. Lola asks you to look for her in the café. What do you do?
Have you ever seen snow?
Yes, in… / No, never.
What did you do?
What sport do you want to learn?
I want to learn to…
Is it expensive?
What languages do you speak?
I speak… and a little…
Where do you use them?
Which is the hardest?
Did you ever get lost as a child?
Yes, once in… / No, never.
Who found you?
Were you scared?
the slope
the beginner
slowly
the little girl (Argentina)
to get lost
This winter it hardly snowed. The lower slopes are green and only the upper ones are open. Hotels are lowering their prices and many instructors, like Lola, are working half the hours.

When I was a girl, in July the snow reached our front door. Now we check the forecast every morning as if it were the lottery. Last year I thought about going to work in Europe, in the Alps, but there is not enough snow there either. Have you noticed changes in the climate where you live?
Lola has few classes this month. What do you advise her?
Offer mountain walks without snow.
Lola organises sunrise walks. Tourists who don’t ski are delighted.
Go to the northern hemisphere in December.
Lola gets work in Canada for their winter. Two winters a year: lots of cold and few holidays.
Give online ski lessons, with videos.
Her “how not to fall” videos get thousands of views. Now people recognise her on the slope.
That night it starts snowing hard and doesn’t stop for three days. Lola’s phone won’t stop ringing.
What was the weather like when you were a child?
Before it was more… / It was the same.
What has changed?
Does it worry you?
Does your work depend on the weather?
Yes, when it rains… / No, not at all.
What do you do on a bad day?
Do you know someone whose does?
Would you work in another country for a season?
Yes, in… / No, because…
What job would you do?
What would you miss?
What did you use to do in the winter holidays?
We used to go to… / I stayed at home and…
Do you still do it?
to snow
the forecast
the sunrise
the season
to miss

The ski resort wants to make artificial snow to secure the season. For that it needs to take millions of litres of water from a mountain stream. Park rangers and some Mapuche communities in the area oppose it. Lola works for the resort, but she is also a volunteer in an environmental group.

My boss asked me to appear in the promotional video for the artificial snow. My friends in the environmental group asked me to sign a letter against it. If I say yes to the video, I lose my friends; if I sign the letter, I might lose my job. How do you get out of this?
Lola has to answer both before Friday. What do you recommend?
Sign the letter and explain to her boss why.
Her boss doesn’t fire her, but gives her the earliest shifts of the whole season.
Do neither.
Nobody is happy. Both sides tell her that having no opinion is also an opinion.
Propose a meeting between the resort and the communities.
The meeting takes place. There is no agreement yet, but for the first time they sit at the same table.
A journalist reports that the resort had already started taking water from the stream before getting the permit. Lola appears in the background of the article’s photo, without knowing it.
Have you had to choose between your job and your beliefs?
Yes, once… / It has never happened to me, but…
What did you choose?
Would you do the same today?
Does tourism help or harm nature?
On the one hand… on the other hand…
What kind of tourism do you prefer?
Who should decide about a region’s water?
I think … should decide.
And if they don’t agree?
What is it like in your country?
Is it possible to be neutral in a conflict like this?
Have you ever been caught in the middle?
How did you feel?
artificial snow
the stream
the park ranger
to fire (from a job)
the permit
The brewery
brewer
It is a wooden bar. There are long tables and many people. Bruno makes the beer here. There is food too.
Hi! I am Bruno. What would you like to drink?
Bruno has three drinks. What do you order?
A blonde beer, please.
Bruno says: “It is light and fresh. Cheers!”
A dark beer.
Bruno says: “It tastes of coffee and chocolate.”
A lemonade, please.
Bruno says: “Sure! It is homemade, with mint.”
Bruno brings a big pizza. “It is for sharing.” There are eight slices. How many do you eat?
What do you drink with food?
I drink water / juice / wine.
And at a party?
What don’t you like?
Do you like pizza?
What do you like on it?
How many slices do you eat?
Do you go to bars with friends?
Yes, on Fridays. / No, I prefer home.
What is your favourite bar?
What do you order?
What food do you share?
I share pizza / chips…
Do you like sharing?
beer
the bar
the slice
homemade
Cheers!
Bariloche has many craft breweries. Bruno makes his beer with mountain water and hops from El Bolsón, a nearby town. At night the place fills up with tired skiers and musicians who play for free.
This beer is called “Nahuelito”. I made it last year and it won a prize. But my favourite is the raspberry one, although hardly anyone orders it. Do you want to try both?
Bruno wants a name for his new beer. What do you suggest?
“Catedral”, like the mountain.
Bruno says there is already one with that name. “Bariloche is small, we all copy!”
“Lola”, after the ski instructor.
Bruno blushes. It seems he likes Lola a lot.
A name in Mapuche.
Bruno decides to ask a teacher from the school to choose the word properly.
The beer fridge breaks. Bruno has forty litres of warm beer and a party in two hours. What do you do?
What typical drink is there in your country?
In my country people drink…
When do people drink it?
What do people do in your city at night?
They go out to… / They stay at home.
And you?
Until what time?
Do you play an instrument?
Yes, I play the… / No, but I would like to.
Since when?
What music do you like?
What name would you give a bar?
I would call it “…” because…
What would the place be like?
What music would there be?
craft / handmade
the prize
raspberry
the fridge (Argentina)
to try / taste

It is Saturday and there is a mountain-cooking contest at the brewery. Each participant prepares a dish with trout, lamb or local mushrooms. Bruno is on the jury, but one of the cooks is his ex-girlfriend.

Look, I’m not going to lie: Carla’s dish is the best. But if I give her the prize, the whole town will say I am still in love. And if I don’t, she will say I hold a grudge. Something similar happened to me two years ago. What would you do?
Bruno has to vote now. What do you tell him?
Vote for the best dish, without thinking about anything else.
Carla wins. Some people whisper, but the lamb really was incredible.
Not vote and explain why.
The audience applauds his honesty. The other two judges choose Carla anyway.
Vote for the second best.
Carla comes second by one point. That night, Bruno can’t sleep.
After the contest, Carla goes up to Bruno and suggests opening a restaurant together, next to the brewery.
Have you ever taken part in a contest?
Yes, a … contest and I won. / Yes, but I didn’t win. / No, never.
Were you nervous?
What did you learn?
Are you friends with an ex?
Yes, we get on well. / No, we prefer not to talk.
Is it possible to be friends?
What do your friends think?
What is the tastiest dish you have tried?
Once I tried… in…
Who cooked it?
Can you make it?
Is it easy to be fair with people you know?
Has it ever happened to you?
the contest
the jury
trout
lamb
resentful / holding a grudge

A big drinks company has bought several craft breweries in Patagonia. Now it is offering Bruno nationwide distribution in every supermarket. It would be a huge success, but he would have to produce ten times more and stop selling only in his bar.

When I started, twelve years ago, I made beer in my mother’s kitchen, in soup pots. My friends told me I was crazy. Now they are offering me what I always dreamed of, and yet I am afraid of becoming just another factory. Craft is not only the recipe: it is the time, the people, this place. Do you think you can grow without losing that?
Bruno has to sign or reject the deal. What do you advise him?
Accept, but with one beer only, and keep the others in the bar.
“Nahuelito” reaches the whole country. The others remain a local secret.
Reject it and grow slowly, with other brewers in the area.
Five breweries set up a cooperative. They earn less, but they decide together.
Accept everything and seize the opportunity.
In one year Bruno earns more than in ten. But he is hardly ever at the bar now and the musicians stop coming.
Bruno discovers that the company has also secretly bought the hop farm in El Bolsón that sells to him and to every brewer in the area.
Can you grow a lot without losing your identity?
Yes, if… / It is hard because…
Do you know an example?
And in people?
What dream did you have when you were young that you haven’t fulfilled yet?
I always wanted to… but…
Is it still possible?
What are you missing?
What do you think of cooperatives?
I think they are… because…
Is there one in your city?
Would you work in one?
Has anyone told you you were crazy because of a project?
Yes, when I wanted to… / No, never.
Were they right?
What would you tell them today?
to distribute
the pot
hops
the cooperative
to take advantage of
The Centro Cívico
tour guide
It is a big square with stone and wooden buildings. There is a tower with a clock. There are big white dogs. Inés is a guide.
Hi, I am Inés. Welcome to Bariloche! Where are you from?
There is a Saint Bernard dog. You can take a photo with the dog. What do you do?
I take a photo with the dog.
Inés says: “What a nice photo! The dog is called Rocco.”
I stroke the dog.
Inés says: “He is very good. He likes it a lot!”
No, thanks. I look at the tower.
Inés says: “The clock is very old.”
The tower clock rings: it is twelve o’clock! Inés asks: “Are you hungry?” What do you say?
Where are you from?
I am from…
What is your city like?
Is there a big square?
Do you like dogs?
Yes, a lot. / I prefer cats.
Do you have a dog?
What is its name?
Do you take many photos?
Yes, many. / No, few.
With your phone?
Of what?
What time is it now?
It is…
What time do you eat?
What time do you go to sleep?
the square
the tower
the clock
the dog
the photo

Bariloche’s Centro Cívico has buildings made of stone and cypress wood, in a style similar to Alpine villages. From the square you can see the lake. Inés gives free guided tours every morning and tourists leave her a tip.
Many tourists think these buildings are old, from Switzerland. But they are from 1940 and an Argentine architect built them! Today I have a group of twelve people from six countries. Will you join?
The tour ends. Inés asks what you want to see next. What do you choose?
The Patagonia museum.
You see objects of the Mapuche and Tehuelche peoples. Inés explains there were no borders here before.
The cathedral, near the lake.
You walk ten minutes along the lakeside. The cathedral has very beautiful stained-glass windows.
A place to eat something typical.
Inés recommends a tea house with Welsh cake and raspberry jam.
A tourist from the group doesn’t tip and leaves quickly. Inés says nothing. What do you do?
Do you take guided tours when you travel?
Yes, always. / No, I prefer going alone.
Which was the best?
Do you leave a tip?
What is the most beautiful building in your city?
For me it is… because…
Is it old?
Can you visit it?
Do you like museums?
Yes, especially … ones. / Not much.
Which is your favourite?
Who do you go with?
Do people tip in your country?
Yes, usually ten per cent. / No, it is not common.
Where?
What do you think about tipping?
the guided tour
the tip
the building
the waterfront
to join

Inés is preparing a new tour about the history of Bariloche. While she looks for information in the city archive, she finds letters from an immigrant family who arrived in 1903. In one of them, a woman tells how she crossed the Andes from Chile in winter, with two children and a cow.

I read the letter three times. This woman walked for twenty days in the snow and then wrote: “We have arrived. The lake is so big it looks like the sea.” And nobody remembers her. The books only talk about the men who founded the city. Do you know how your family came to the place where they live?
How should Inés use these letters?
Read a letter aloud at the end of each tour.
Many tourists are moved. Some write to her afterwards to tell their own family’s story.
Look for the family’s descendants.
She finds a great-granddaughter who lives three blocks away. She knew nothing about the letters.
Suggest an exhibition to the museum.
The museum accepts, but says it will take a year. Inés starts writing the texts that same night.
In the last letter, the woman mentions “Mrs Inés, who helped us cross.” It is the same name as the guide, and she was her great-great-grandmother.
Do you know where your family came from?
My grandparents / great-grandparents came from…
Why did they leave?
Who told you?
Do you keep old letters or photos?
Yes, I have… from my… / No, everything is on my phone.
Which is the oldest?
Where do you keep them?
What difficult journey did someone in your family make?
My… travelled to… in…
How long did it take?
Why did they do it?
Who deserves to be in history books and isn’t?
I think… because…
Why do you think they aren’t?
What did they do?
the archive
the letter
the mountain range
the descendant
the great-granddaughter

In the Centro Cívico square there is a statue of a 19th-century military officer. For many he is a national hero; for the Mapuche communities, he is responsible for the violent occupation of their lands. One group wants it removed, another wants it protected. The town council asks Inés, as a guide, to propose the text for a new sign next to the statue.

Every day, in front of that statue, someone asks me who he was. If I say “a hero”, some get angry; if I say “a perpetrator of genocide”, others do. I believe a guide is not there to tell people what to think, but to give the full picture. But how do you sum up a hundred years of conflict in fifty words? What would you write?
Inés has to present her proposal tomorrow. What do you suggest?
A sign with both views, side by side.

Between 1845 and 1852 a million Irish people died of hunger and another million emigrated. My great-grandmother was one of those who left for America. It is seven in the morning. Declan arrives before the tourist buses. On the path there is a sign: “Danger. Do not pass.” On the other side of the sign, a boy sits on the edge for a photo.

I have worked here for twelve years. More than two thousand people come every day. Almost all of them are responsible, but there is always someone who wants the perfect photo. I prefer boring photos and living tourists. Would you do something dangerous for a photo?
The boy does not listen to Declan. What do you do?
I talk to him calmly and ask him to come back.
The boy comes back. He is embarrassed, but he thanks you.
I offer to take a better photo of him from here.
The photo comes out very well. He posts it online with your name.
I call another guide.
Two guides arrive and the boy leaves angry.
The park wants to put a high metal fence along the whole edge. It is safer, but the photos will not be the same. Do you agree?
Do you always respect danger signs?
Always. / Almost always, but once…
What happened?
Would you do it again?
What is the most beautiful landscape you have seen?
I saw… in…
Who did you go with?
Would you go back?
What time do you get up when you travel?
I get up early / late.
And at home?
Are you a morning or a night person?
What outdoor job would you like?
I would like to be…
And in bad weather?
What is the hard part?
the edge
the danger
the sign
the fence
to be embarrassed

It is late and there is almost nobody left. Declan takes you to O’Brien’s Tower, a small nineteenth-century stone tower. From the top you can see the Aran Islands. Declan tells you that when he was young he wanted to move to Canada.

At twenty-two I had the ticket to Toronto bought. My two brothers were already there. The night before the trip my father got ill and I stayed. At first I was furious, but then I found this job and I never left. Sometimes I think about the other life I didn’t have. Has something like that happened to you?
Declan has a job offer in Canada now, at forty-three. What do you tell him?
To go: it is never too late.
Declan laughs nervously. “My mother is going to kill me,” he says, but he keeps the email.
To go for a month first, as a test.
He thinks it is a good idea. He asks for holidays in winter.
To stay: he is happy here.
Declan looks at the sea for a while and says: “You are right. I think.”
Declan confesses that his brother in Toronto is coming back to Ireland: he lost his job and got divorced. “He wanted my life and I wanted his,” he says. What do you think about that?
Have you ever changed plans because of your family?
Yes, when… / No, never.
What did you learn?
Do you have family living in another country?
Yes, my uncle lives in… / No.
Why did they leave?
Do you visit them?
At what age is it too late to start again?
I think never / at…
Do you know someone who started late?
Did it go well?
What other life do you sometimes imagine?
Sometimes I imagine myself living in… / working as…
What stops you?
Are you going to try?
the ticket
to stay
to regret
the offer
as a trial

The county council is debating a project: a new visitor centre with a glass lift down to the base of the cliffs and a café hanging over the sea. It would bring hundreds of jobs. Environmentalists say it would destroy the bird colonies. Declan has to speak at the meeting tomorrow.

They asked me to speak as a guide, not as a neighbour. The problem is that I think different things depending on the day. On Monday I see the village kids leaving for Dublin because there is no work. On Tuesday I see a puffin with its chick and I think the lift is madness. If you had to write my speech, where would you start?
What position do you recommend Declan takes at the meeting?
Support the project with strict conditions for the birds.
The environmentalists call him a traitor, but the council includes his conditions in the contract.
Oppose it and propose smaller tourism spread along the coast.
Hotel owners get angry. A local paper puts his proposal on the front page.
Not take sides and ask for an independent study.
The vote is delayed a year. Nobody is happy, but nobody hates him.

That night, Declan finds out that the construction company belongs to his cousin. If he speaks against it, the family will not forgive him; if he speaks in favour, everyone will say he did it for his cousin. Should he speak anyway or withdraw?
What matters more to you: jobs for people or protecting nature?
For me… although I understand that…
Is there a case like this in your country?
What was decided?
Would you speak publicly against a family project?
Yes, if it were necessary. / No, I would talk privately first.
What would be hardest for you?
Has something similar happened to you?
Do you change your mind easily?
Yes, if I get good arguments. / Hardly ever.
What did you change your mind about?
Who convinced you?
Should famous natural places limit visits?
They should… because otherwise…
How would you do it?
Would you pay more to get in?
the council
the speech
to take sides
to withdraw
the chick / young
The festival in the streets of Galway
street performer
It is July in Galway. The street is full of people. There is music, colours and balloons. Niamh is painted silver. She does not move: she is a statue.
… Hello! I scared you! I am Niamh. I am a living statue. Put in a coin and I move.
Niamh waits. What do you do?
I put in a coin.
Niamh dances like a robot. People clap.
I take a photo with her.
Niamh shakes your hand with her silver hand. Now your hand is silver!
I stay still like her.
Now there are two statues. The children laugh a lot.
It starts to rain. Niamh’s paint is coming off! What do you do?
Do you like festivals?
Yes, a lot. / No, there are too many people.
Which festival do you know?
When is it?
Do you give money to street artists?
Yes, sometimes. / No, never.
Which ones?
How much?
Can you stay still for a long time?
Yes, I can. / No, I move a lot.
How many minutes?
Shall we try now?
What colour do you like?
I like…
Do you have clothes in that colour?
And your home?
the statue
the coin
still
the paint
the balloon
It is five in the morning. Niamh paints herself in front of a van mirror. It takes her an hour. Then she goes to Shop Street, the most touristy one, to get a good spot before the other artists.

I studied theatre at university, but theatre doesn’t pay the rent. On the street I earn more on a good Saturday than in a month of theatre. The hard part isn’t staying still: it’s not scratching when your nose itches. What do you do when something itches and you can’t scratch?
A musician with a drum sets up right next to Niamh. He makes a lot of noise. What do you advise her?
Talk to him and share the hours.
He plays from ten to twelve and she from twelve to two. It works.
Do an act together.
The statue moves to the rhythm of the drum. They earn double!
Change street.
On the other street there are fewer people. Niamh earns little that day.
The city council wants street artists to pay a permit of a hundred euros a year. Do you think it is fair?
What did you study or what do you want to study?
I studied… / I want to study…
Do you work in that?
Why did you choose it?
What time do you start work?
I start at…
Is that early for you?
How do you get there?
Which street artist do you remember?
I remember a… in…
What did they do?
Did you give them money?
Do you prefer a secure job or a job you like?
I prefer… because…
And your job now?
Can you have both?
the mirror
the rent
to itch
to scratch
the permit

It is the last day of the festival. Niamh invites you to see the big parade: giant puppets, drums and hundreds of dancers. Before that, in a café, she tells you that last year she almost gave everything up to work in an office.

Last winter was horrible. It rained almost every day and I earned very little. I sent CVs to companies and a bank called me. I went to the interview in a suit, without silver paint! They offered me the job. That night I couldn’t sleep. What do you think I did?
Niamh asks you to guess. What do you say?
That she accepted and worked a few months.
“Almost! I worked three weeks. I cried in the bathroom every day,” Niamh says.
That she said no the next day.
“No, I was more of a coward: I never answered,” she says, and laughs.
That she did both.
“That’s what I do now: bank in winter, street in summer. And I’m happy.”
In the parade, a giant puppet breaks and a huge head falls in the middle of the street. The organisers need volunteers to carry it. Niamh looks at you. Do you help?
Have you ever left a job or a course?
Yes, I left… because… / No, never.
How did you feel afterwards?
Was it a good decision?
What was your strangest job interview like?
They asked me… and I said…
Did you get the job?
What were you wearing?
What was last winter like for you?
It was… because…
What did you do at weekends?
Are you hoping for a better one?
Which popular festival from your country do you recommend?
I recommend… because there are…
Did you go?
What do people eat?
the parade
the puppet
the interview
the job / position
the volunteer

A video of Niamh went viral: millions of people watched her hold a pose during a storm. Now an agency offers her a contract to advertise an energy drink brand, dressed as a statue. Her street colleagues think she has sold out before she has signed anything.

The funny thing is that I was still that day because I was so cold I couldn’t move. Now everyone wants something from me. The agency would pay me in a month what I earn in two years, but I would have to say lines I didn’t write and do what they say. My friends say the street is free and that is priceless. What would you do with fifteen minutes of fame?
Niamh has to answer today. What do you advise her?
Sign for one year and save everything for her own project.
Niamh signs. At the end of the year she opens a small street theatre school.
Negotiate: accept only if she can write her own acts.
The agency accepts half of her conditions. The first ad is surprisingly good.
Refuse and use the fame to fill her hat on the street.
For a month she earns a lot, but then people forget the video.
Niamh discovers that the drink has so much caffeine that it is banned for minors in several countries, and that the ad is aimed at teenagers. Should she go ahead if she has already signed?
What would you do if a video of yours went viral tomorrow?
First… and then I would try to…
Which video would you be afraid of going viral?
Is it “selling out” to accept money from a big company?
It depends on… / No, because we all need…
Where is your limit?
Have you ever crossed it?
Would you break a contract for ethical reasons?
Yes, even if I had to pay… / No, a contract is a contract.
What reason would be enough?
Do you know a real case?
What is worth more than money in a job?
For me… is worth more because…
Does your current job have it?
Did any job have it?
to go viral
fame
to sell out
to negotiate
the advert
The fields of Connemara
pony breeder
It is a green and brown field. There are lakes, mountains and sheep. Padraig has six grey ponies. He wears rubber boots.
Good morning. I am Padraig. These are my ponies. They are small but very strong. Do you want to touch one?
What do you do with the pony?
I give it an apple.
The pony eats the apple and wants another.
I touch it carefully.
The pony closes its eyes. It is calm.
I get on the pony.
Padraig says: “Slowly!” You go for a short ride.
A little pony escapes across the field. Padraig runs. What do you do?
Do you like horses?
Yes, a lot. / No, they scare me.
Have you ridden one?
Where?
Do you prefer the countryside or the city?
I prefer the countryside / the city.
Where do you live?
Do you have rain boots?
Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.
Does it rain a lot where you live?
Do you like rain?
What fruit do you like?
I like apples / pears…
Do you eat fruit every day?
Which one don’t you like?
the pony
the sheep
the lake
the boots
slowly

Padraig is cutting turf in the field, as his grandfather did. Turf is black earth that dries in the sun and is burned in the fireplace. It smells of smoke and wet earth. Next to it there is a small house with a thatched roof.

I cut the turf in May, dry it in June and take it home in August. In winter I burn it and the house has a special smell. My daughter says it is bad for the planet and she is right, but for me it is the smell of my childhood. What smell reminds you of your childhood?
Padraig gives you a spade. What do you do?
I cut turf with him.
After ten minutes your back hurts. Padraig laughs.
I prefer taking photos of the landscape.
The sun comes out for a moment and the mountains look golden.
I ask him about the thatched house.
It is his grandmother’s house. Inside there is an old stove and old photos.
The government wants to ban turf cutting to protect the bogs. What do you think?
What smell reminds you of your childhood?
The smell of… reminds me of…
Where do you smell it today?
Is it a nice memory?
How do you heat your home in winter?
With central heating / with a stove…
Is it expensive?
Do you have a fireplace?
Do you do anything the same as your grandparents?
Yes, I cook like my grandmother / No, nothing.
Who taught you?
Will you teach it?
Have you ever worked in the countryside?
Yes, once… / No, never.
Was it hard?
the turf / peat
the spade
the smoke
the straw / thatch
the smell

It is the Clifden pony show. There are breeders from all over the country, judges in hats and children leading ponies on ropes. Padraig is showing Ciara, his best mare. He is nervous: he has not won a prize for ten years.

My father won here seven times. I won only once, the year he died, and I dedicated the prize to him. Since then, nothing. My neighbours say the judges prefer rich breeders. I don’t know if that is true or an excuse. Have you ever taken part in a competition?
Ciara is nervous before going in. What do you advise Padraig?
Walk with her for a while away from the people.
Ciara calms down. She goes in calmly and walks very well.
Let his granddaughter take her, she has known her since she was little.
The girl goes in with Ciara and the crowd applauds a lot.
Not take part this year.
Padraig says no. “My father never pulled out,” he says, and goes in.
Ciara comes second. An American buyer offers three times the normal price for her. Padraig needs the money to fix the roof. Does he sell her?
Have you ever won a prize or a competition?
Yes, I won… when… / No, I never won anything.
How did you feel?
What did you do with the prize?
Do people compare you with someone in your family?
Yes, with my sister… / No, luckily.
Does it bother you?
How are you different?
Would you sell something you love out of need?
If necessary, yes. / I would never sell…
What would you never sell?
Do you get nervous before something important?
Yes, very. / Not much.
What do you do to calm down?
Does it work?
the show / fair
the judge
the mare
the prize
the buyer

Padraig is sixty-eight and none of his children want to carry on the farm. A German couple wants to buy it to make an eco-hotel. His neighbour, on the other hand, wants to buy it cheaply to join it to his land and keep raising animals. Padraig is sitting in the kitchen with the two offers on the table.

This land has been in my family since the time of the Great Famine. My great-grandfather stayed when half the village left for America. If I sell it to the Germans, my children will have money, but the farm will stop being a farm. If I sell it to my neighbour, there will still be ponies, but my children will reproach me for giving away their inheritance. What weighs more: history or the future of those who remain?
What do you recommend to Padraig?
Sell to the neighbour and explain to his children why.
Two of his children understand; the third stops calling him for a while.
Sell to the German couple on condition they keep the ponies.
The couple accepts and hires Padraig to look after the animals two days a week.
Not sell yet and offer the farm to young people who want to learn.
A very determined girl from Galway arrives. Padraig doesn’t know whether to trust her.
His youngest daughter calls from Australia: she says she might come back in five years to take over the farm, but she is not sure. Should Padraig wait for a promise that may not be kept?
Is there something in your family passed from generation to generation?
Yes, a house / a recipe / a business…
Who will inherit it?
Do you want it?
Do children have an obligation to continue their parents’ work?
No, because everyone… / Partly, if…
What did your parents expect of you?
Did you do it?
Would you wait five years for a promise?
It depends on who… / No, because life…
Has anyone promised you something they didn’t keep?
Did you forgive them?
What is happening to the small villages in your country?
Many are running out of… because…
Are there solutions?
Would you live in one?
the farm
the inheritance
to reproach
the famine
to keep a promise
The oyster festival
oyster farmer
It is September. There is a big tent by the sea. There are tables, lemons and brown bread. Eoin opens oysters with a small knife.
Hello! I am Eoin. These are Galway oysters. They are from the sea here. Do you eat oysters?
Eoin offers you an oyster. What do you do?
I eat it with lemon.
“Do you like it?” Eoin asks. It tastes of the sea.
I prefer the bread.
Eoin gives you bread with butter. It is very tasty.
No, thank you. I don’t like them.
Eoin says: “No problem. A fish soup?”
There is a contest: who can open the most oysters in one minute? Eoin gives you a knife. Do you take part?
Do you like fish?
Which one?
How do you eat it?
Do you eat new food when you travel?
Yes, always. / No, I prefer normal food.
What did you eat?
Did you like it?
What food don’t you like?
I don’t like…
Since when?
Did you try it again?
Do you cook at home?
Yes, every day. / No, hardly ever.
What do you cook?
For whom?
the oyster
the lemon
the knife
the tent / marquee
to taste of

It is early and the tide is low. Eoin walks across the sand in tall boots between rows of black bags. The oysters grow inside the bags. They take three years to be ready. It is cold and the sky is grey.

I work with the tide, not with the clock. Some days I start at four in the morning and others at three in the afternoon. My girlfriend says I am impossible to make plans with. The best thing about the job is the silence; the worst, frozen hands. Does your job have fixed hours?
Eoin needs help turning the bags. What do you do?
I put on some boots and help.
You work for an hour. At the end Eoin gives you a dozen oysters.
I ask him how oysters grow.
Eoin explains that an oyster cleans many litres of water every day.
I stay in the car with the heating on.
From the car you see Eoin alone on the beach. It looks like a painting.
A Dublin restaurant wants to buy all of Eoin’s oysters at a good price. But then he would have no oysters for the village festival. What do you tell him?
Does your work or study have fixed hours?
Yes, from… to… / No, it changes a lot.
Do you like it like that?
What would you change?
What is the best and worst thing about your job?
The best is… and the worst is…
Was it always like that?
Do you recommend it?
Did you ever get up very early for something special?
Yes, to see… / for a trip…
Was it worth it?
Do you buy local food or supermarket food?
I shop at the market / at the supermarket.
Is it more expensive?
Do you notice the difference?
the tide
the sand
to grow
frozen
the dozen

It is the final of the oyster-opening championship. Eoin is competing against a French chef and a village grandfather who has won four times. The crowd shouts, there are journalists and a band is playing. Eoin practised all year, but this morning he cut a finger.

I have a bandage on and it hurts when I squeeze. My coach, who is my uncle, says I shouldn’t compete. But it is the first time I have reached the final. When I was a boy I watched that grandfather win and I wanted to be like him. Have you ever done something important while in pain or ill?
What do you tell Eoin?
To compete, but calmly, without going for the record.
Eoin comes third. The grandfather hugs him and tells him next year is his.
To use the other hand: he practised it in secret.
He is slower, but makes no mistakes. He comes second!
Not to compete and go to the doctor.
The doctor gives him three stitches. Eoin watches the final from the crowd, sad.
After the final, a journalist says the French chef used an illegal knife. The judges did not see it. Eoin has a video that proves it. Does he show it?
Did you do something important while ill or in pain?
Yes, once I went to… with a fever.
How did it go?
Was it a good idea?
Who did you admire as a child?
I admired… because…
Do you still admire them?
Did you meet them?
Would you report someone who cheated?
Yes, always. / It depends on…
And if they are your friend?
Have you ever seen cheating?
Did you practise a lot for something?
Yes, I practised… for…
How much time a day?
Did you achieve it?
the championship
the bandage
to cut oneself
to cheat
the judges / jury

A laboratory found a bacterium in the bay’s waters after the rains. It is not certain it affects Eoin’s oysters, but the authorities recommend not selling them for three weeks, just before the festival. If he waits, he loses the season; if he sells, he risks people’s health and his name.

It is a recommendation, not a ban. My own tests came out clean, but I paid for my tests myself, so I understand if someone is suspicious. Two other producers are going to sell anyway. If I don’t sell and they do, I lose my customers; if I sell and someone gets sick, it’s all over. How do you decide when nobody knows the truth?
What do you advise Eoin?
Not sell and explain it publicly at the festival.
He loses a lot of money, but a newspaper presents him as an example of a responsible producer.
Pay for an urgent independent test and decide with that result.
The test is expensive and takes five days. It comes out clean. He sells late, but with peace of mind.
Sell only cooked oysters, which are safer.
The purists complain, but the tent fills with curious people.
One of the producers who sold anyway now has customers in hospital. The authorities close the whole bay, including for Eoin, for six months. Is it fair that everyone pays for one person’s decision?
How do you make decisions when you don’t have all the information?
Usually… / I prefer to wait until…
Have you ever got it wrong that way?
Do you trust the authorities’ recommendations?
Generally yes, although… / Not much, because…
On which topic do you trust them most?
And least?
Is it fair that everyone pays for one person’s mistake?
No, only… should pay / Sometimes it is necessary because…
Did it happen to you at school or work?
How did you react?
Would you lose money to protect your reputation?
Yes, because reputation… / It depends how much…
Which company lost its reputation?
Did it get it back?
the bay
the season
to risk
the test / analysis
the reputation
The Ring of Kerry road
bus driver
It is a narrow road. On one side there are mountains and on the other side is the sea. Tadhg drives a green bus. There are twenty tourists.
Good morning! I am Tadhg. Today we go around the Ring of Kerry. It is a hundred and eighty kilometres. Are you ready?
Where do you sit?
At the front, near Tadhg.
Tadhg tells you stories the whole trip.
By the window, on the sea side.
You see beaches, islands and a rainbow.
At the back, to sleep.
You sleep for an hour. You miss the views!
There are sheep on the road. The bus stops. The sheep don’t move. What do you do?
Do you like travelling by bus?
Yes, a lot. / No, I prefer the car.
Where do you go by bus?
How long?
Where do you sit on the bus?
At the front. / By the window. / At the back.
Why?
Do you sleep on the bus?
Have you seen a rainbow?
Yes, in… / No, never.
Who were you with?
Did you take a photo?
Do you have a car?
Yes, I do. / No, I don’t.
What colour is it?
Do you like driving?
the road
narrow
to drive
the rainbow
the view
The bus stops at a viewpoint. The tourists get off to take photos. Tadhg drinks tea from his flask. There is an old man selling sweaters and a dog that helps move the sheep.

I have made this trip five times a week for fifteen years. It is always the same road, but never the same day: the light changes, the weather changes, the people change. The buses always go the same way, anticlockwise, so they don’t meet on the bends. Do you repeat any route every day?
A tourist hasn’t come back to the bus. Ten minutes have passed. What do you advise Tadhg?
Wait five more minutes.
The tourist arrives running with a new sweater. Everyone claps.
Go and look for him.
You find him talking to the dog. “He is very clever!” he says.
Leave without him.
Tadhg says: “I never leave anyone.” And he waits.
Tadhg says that many tourists now hire cars and don’t want a bus. His company may close. What do you recommend?
What route do you take every day?
I go from home to… by…
How long does it take?
Does it bore you?
Do you prefer travelling alone or with a group?
I prefer… because…
Have you done a group tour?
How was it?
Are you often late?
Yes, always. / No, I am punctual.
Has anyone waited for you?
Do you wait for others?
What do you always take on a long trip?
I always take water, music…
And what do you always forget?
Do you take food?
the viewpoint
the flask
the bend
to hire / rent
punctual

It is the last trip of the season. The bus is almost empty: just you, a Japanese couple and an eighty-year-old lady coming back to Kerry after sixty years in Boston. She wants to see the house where she lived as a girl.

Mrs Kathleen gave me an old photo of her house. She says it was near a white church and a bridge, but in Kerry there are many white churches and many bridges. It is not a stop on the route. If I make a detour, we will be late for dinner at the hotel. What would you do?
Tadhg asks the passengers. How do you vote?
Make the detour: dinner can wait.
After an hour they find the house. It is in ruins, but Kathleen cries with joy.
Ask in a village pub first.
A man in the pub recognises the surname. He is Kathleen’s cousin!
Come back tomorrow by taxi.
Kathleen agrees, but at the hotel she can’t sleep from nerves.
A young family from Poland now lives in the house. They invite Kathleen for tea in the kitchen where she ate as a girl. She doesn’t know whether to go in. What do you tell her?
Have you ever gone back to your childhood home?
Yes, and it was… / No, it doesn’t exist any more.
What did you feel?
Who lives there now?
Do you have family who moved to another country long ago?
Yes, my great-grandparents came from… / Not that I know of.
Why did they leave?
Do you know that place?
Would you change a plan to help a stranger?
Yes, if… / It depends on…
Have you ever done it?
How did it end?
Do you keep old family photos?
Yes, I have an album… / They are at my mother’s house.
Which is your favourite?
Who is in it?
to make a detour
the route
the surname
in ruins
the passenger

Tadhg’s company wants to replace the big buses with small electric vans and an app that explains the landscape with audio. Drivers who tell stories would no longer be needed: the app does it in twelve languages. Tadhg is offered an office job or a redundancy payment.

The app knows dates and names better than I do, that is true. But it doesn’t know that the lady at the café in Waterville lost her husband last month and that you have to stop and say hello to her. It doesn’t know which joke works with Germans and which with Argentinians. Can a machine do a job that is really about knowing people?
What do you recommend to Tadhg?
Accept the office job and help improve the app with his stories.
He records a hundred stories for the app. Tourists ask who “the voice of Kerry” is.
Take the redundancy money and start his own tour for small groups.
He starts with an old van. The first summer goes well; the winter is very hard.
Organise the drivers to negotiate a different model with the company.
The company agrees to have drivers on half the routes, at least for two years.
The company’s surveys show that young tourists prefer the app: they can stop when they want and don’t have to talk to anyone. Does it make sense to defend something customers no longer ask for?
What jobs do you think a machine can’t do?
I think no machine can… because…
And in twenty years?
Is your job at risk?
Do you prefer a human guide or an audio guide?
I prefer… because I can…
Do you remember a special guide?
What did they have?
What would you do with a large redundancy payment?
I would use it to… / I would save it…
Would you risk your own business?
What business?
Should traditional jobs be protected even if they are less efficient?
Yes, because they bring… / No, the world changes and…
What job disappeared in your country?
Is it missed?
the redundancy payment

The boat to Skellig Michael

It is a small boat in the harbour. The sea is moving a lot. Far away there is a very high rock island. Fionnuala is the skipper.
Hello! I am Fionnuala. We are going to Skellig island. There are ancient monks and lots of birds. Do you get seasick on boats?
The sea is moving. What do you do?
I look at the horizon.
You feel better. You see dolphins next to the boat.
I eat a biscuit.
Fionnuala says: “Very good. Bread and biscuits, yes.”
I sit inside.
Inside you can’t see the sea. You feel sicker!
On the island there are six hundred stone steps. They are very steep. Do you climb?
Do you like boats?
Yes, a lot. / No, I get seasick.
Where did you go by boat?
Have you ever seen dolphins?
How many?
Would you like to?
Do you like climbing stairs?
Yes, it is good exercise. / No, I prefer the lift.
What floor do you live on?
Is there a lift?
What do you see from your window?
I see a street / a park / the sea…
Do you like it?
What would you like to see?

At the top of the island there are little beehive-shaped stone huts. Fourteen hundred years ago about twelve monks lived here. They had no trees, no soil, almost nothing. Fionnuala shows you the small garden they made among the rocks.

The monks ate fish, birds’ eggs and the little that grew here. In winter no boat came for months. They lived in silence, prayed and copied books. I come in summer and after two hours I already want my coffee. Could you live without internet or shops for a week?
Fionnuala gives you ten free minutes. What do you do?
I sit in silence, like the monks.
You only hear the wind and the birds. It is very strange and very beautiful.
I go into a stone hut.
Inside it is dark and there is no wind. Only one person lying down fits.
I look for puffins for a photo.
A puffin stands still in front of you, like a model.
Fionnuala says they filmed a Star Wars movie here, and now many more people come. Is it good or bad for the island?
Could you live a week without internet?
Yes, no problem. / No, impossible.
What would you do?
What would you miss most?
Do you like silence?
Yes, it relaxes me. / No, it makes me nervous.
Where do you find silence?
Do you always listen to music?
Have you visited a place from a film?
Yes, I went to… / No, but I want to go to…
Which film?
Was it like on screen?
What would you eat on an island without shops?
I would eat fish, eggs…
Can you fish?
Can you cook over a fire?

to pray

It is time to go back, but the wind has suddenly changed. The waves are bigger and Fionnuala is talking to the harbour on the radio. There is another boat with twelve tourists who haven’t come down from the island yet. An older tourist has twisted her ankle on the steps.

I have been on this sea for twenty years and learned only one rule: the sea decides, not me. Three years ago we had to leave a group on the island for a night because it was impossible to get back. They were cold and scared, but they all came back. Today the harbour tells me I have an hour, maybe less. What would you do first?
Fionnuala needs help. What do you do?
I go up to help the lady with the ankle come down.
They come down very slowly with three people. They reach the boat just in time.
I stay on the boat and hand out life jackets.
Everyone is ready when the group arrives. Fionnuala leaves immediately.
I call the coastguard.
A helicopter comes for the lady. The rest go back by boat, wet but fine.
Back in the harbour, a tourist complains because he couldn’t see the whole island and asks for his money back. Fionnuala is exhausted. What would you say to that tourist?
Have you ever been in a dangerous situation?
Yes, once… / Luckily, no.
Who helped you?
What did you learn?
How do you react in an emergency?
I stay calm / I get nervous…
Do you know first aid?
Where did you learn?
Have you ever complained on a trip?
Yes, because the hotel… / No, I never complain.
Did they give you your money back?
Were you right?
What rules have you learned from experience?
I learned that you should never…
Who taught it to you?
Do you always follow it?

Skellig Michael is a World Heritage Site. To protect it, the government only allows a hundred and eighty visitors a day and fifteen licensed boats. Fionnuala holds one of those licences, which passed from her father to her. Now a travel platform is offering to pay any price for the licences and sell them to rich tourists as an “exclusive experience”.

My father took anyone: students, priests, grandmothers from Cork. He charged little because he said the island wasn’t his, he was only the way there. The platform is offering me more money than I will earn in my whole life. Three licences have already been sold. If I sell, I retire tomorrow. If I don’t, I may be the last local skipper in this harbour. Does it make sense to resist when the others have already given in?
What do you advise Fionnuala?
Not sell and ask the government to ban selling licences to companies.
The proposal reaches parliament. It is slow, but other skippers join in.
Sell, but demand that one day a week is at an affordable price.
The platform accepts it in the contract, but nobody checks whether it complies.
Create a cooperative with the remaining skippers.
They share boats, customers and costs. They earn less, but nobody else sells.

A scientific study says the boats harm the bird colonies and recommends closing the island to the public for ten years. Then the licences would be worth nothing. Should Fionnuala sell now, before it becomes known?
Should unique places be for whoever can pay most?
No, because… / Partly, if the money is used to…
Which place in your country is like this?
How much does it cost?
Would you use information others don’t have to make money?
I don’t think it’s fair because… / If it’s legal, yes.
Where is the line?
Do you know a case?
Is it worth resisting when everyone else gives in?
Yes, because someone has to… / No, it’s pointless if…
Have you ever resisted?
Would you close a famous place for ten years to protect it?
Yes, if experts say… / No, because local people…
Who should decide?
How would you compensate local people?

to retire
to give in

Hello! I am Mick, and this is Bruno. Shall we take a ride through the park? It is thirty minutes.

I give Bruno water.

Do you like parks?

The cart passes Muckross House, an old mansion with gardens. Mick talks the whole time: he tells stories, jokes and facts about every tree. Some are true and others, you suspect, are made up.

Queen Victoria visited this house in 1861. The owners spent a fortune getting it ready and afterwards were almost poor. She only stayed two nights. That is true, eh? The one about the ghost in the kitchen… that one I’m not so sure about. Do you like ghost stories?
Mick says he can tell a scary story or a love story. Which do you choose?
The scary one.
Mick talks about a cook who still makes tea at night. Bruno neighs and everyone laughs.
The love one.
It is the story of a gardener and the owner’s daughter. It ends badly, of course.
A story from his life.
Mick goes quiet for a moment and tells how he met his wife on this path.
Some tourists say using horses for tourists is cruel. Mick gets angry. What do you think?
Do you believe in ghosts?
Yes, a little. / No, not at all.
Do you know a story?
Does it scare you?

I met them at…

It is Sunday and there is a cart race in the town. Mick hasn’t competed for years, but his nephew Seán persuaded him to lend him Bruno. Bruno is already nineteen. The vet says he is fine, although Mick isn’t so sure.

Bruno won this race three times when he was young. My nephew is a good lad, but he wants to win at all costs, like me at his age. Last night I didn’t sleep thinking about the bends in the road. Part of me wants to see him win again, and part of me wants to pull him out of the race. What would you do with an old animal?
There are ten minutes to go. What do you tell Mick?
To talk to Seán and ask him to take it easy.
Seán promises not to push him. They come fourth and Bruno finishes happy.
To drive himself, like before.
Mick and Bruno race together one last time. The crowd gives them a standing ovation.
To withdraw Bruno: it’s not worth it.
Seán gets angry, but the next day he brings Bruno a bag of carrots.
After the race, a luxury hotel wants to buy Bruno so the guests’ children can take photos with him. They would give him good food and little work. Does Mick sell him?
Have you had an animal that grew old?
Yes, my dog… / No, I never had animals.
How did you look after it?
Do you remember it a lot?
Did you want to win at all costs when you were young?
Yes, I was very competitive. / No, I never cared.
And now?
What changed?
Have you lent something important to a relative?
Yes, I lent my car / my house…
Did they give it back in good condition?
Would you do it again?
Is there a famous race or competition in your city?
Yes, every year there is… / Not that I know of.
Have you taken part?
Do you go and watch?

An animal rights group has launched a campaign to ban jaunting cars in the park, as has already happened in other cities. It has fifty thousand signatures. The drivers say their horses live better than many pets. The council has invited Mick to a debate on local radio.

My family has had horses in this park for five generations. Bruno eats better than me, goes to the vet more than me and works four hours a day. But I understand that someone who sees him in the heat, on the road, among cars, might think he is suffering. What bothers me is that most of the people who signed have never been here. Can you have an opinion on something you don’t know up close?
What strategy do you recommend for the debate?
Invite the group to spend a day with Bruno.
Two activists accept. One changes her mind; the other doesn’t, but softens her tone.
Propose new rules: fewer hours, no work in the heat, public inspections.
The council adopts the rules. Some drivers complain that Mick gave in too much.
Defend the tradition with facts and give no ground.
The debate gets tense. The radio receives hundreds of messages, for and against.

The day before the debate, another driver’s horse collapses from the heat and the video spreads across social media. Mick knows that driver doesn’t look after his animals well. Should he say so publicly, even though he is a colleague?
Can you have an opinion on something you don’t know up close?
Yes, but carefully… / No, first you need to…
Did you change your mind afterwards?
Do you sign online petitions?
Sometimes, when… / No, because they don’t work.
What was the last one?
Did it achieve anything?
Is using animals for work acceptable today?
It depends on the animal and… / No, never, because…
And police dogs or guide dogs?
Where do you draw the line?
Would you criticise a colleague in public?
Only if… / I prefer to talk privately because…
What happened when you did?
And if they criticise you?

It is a very long beach. The water is cold. Róisín has a black wetsuit and a yellow board. There are six students on the sand.
Hello! I am Róisín. Today we learn to surf. The water is cold: eleven degrees. Are you ready?

I go into the water straight away.
It is very cold! You shout and everyone laughs.
I practise on the sand first.
Róisín says: “Perfect! Up, down, up.”
I watch the others.
A student falls ten times. You learn by watching.

Can you swim?
Yes, well. / A little. / No.

Where?
What other sport do you want to learn?

The class is over. Róisín and the students are having hot soup from a food van on the beach. Everyone has red hands from the cold. A fifty-five-year-old student stood up on the board for the first time and can’t stop smiling.

I started surfing at twelve with my brother’s broken board. In Ireland people think surfing is for Australia or California, but here we have incredible waves and almost nobody in the water. My favourite student today is fifty-five. It is never too late. What would you like to learn even if it embarrasses you?
The fifty-five-year-old student asks you if she should continue with the classes. What do you tell her?
Yes, every week.
She buys a new wetsuit. Róisín gives her a discount.
To try in summer, when it is less cold.
She says: “In summer there are too many people. I’m coming back on Saturday!”

Her husband comes the following week. He never stands up, but he has lots of fun.
Róisín wants to open a surf school just for women over forty. Some people say it is discrimination. What do you think?

I have soup / hot chocolate…

It is a stormy day and the school is closed. Róisín invites you to her home, a caravan next to the beach. She has photos of waves on every wall and a medal from a national championship. She tells you why she stopped competing.

At twenty-four I was the second-best surfer in Ireland. I had sponsors and travelled to Portugal and France. One day, on a huge wave, I hit the rocks and broke my shoulder. I spent a year without going into the water. When I came back, I didn’t want to win any more: I wanted to enjoy it. Has an accident or illness ever changed something for you?
A brand offers her a return to competition in a veterans’ championship. What do you advise her?
To accept, just for fun.
Róisín competes without pressure and wins. She celebrates with her students.
To accept, but take her students as a team.
The brand agrees. Three students compete for the first time.
To say no: she is happy teaching now.
Róisín hangs the letter on the wall, next to the medal.
While you are talking, someone knocks on the door: a boy has gone into the sea in the storm and can’t get out. Róisín grabs her board. Do you go with her or call emergency services?
Did an accident or illness change something for you?
Yes, after… I started to… / No, luckily.
Was it for the better?

I prefer… but sometimes…
Was it always like that?

Where is it?

Yes, I would love it. / No, I need…

A company wants to build an artificial wave pool fifteen kilometres from the beach: perfect waves every day, without cold or storms, with a café and a shop. It offers Róisín the job of director of the school, with a fixed salary for the first time in her life. Her surfer friends say that isn’t surfing, it’s an amusement park.

In the sea you learn to wait, to read the wind, to feel fear and respect. In a pool you learn technique in half the time, with no danger. My older students would be delighted: no currents and no eleven-degree water. But I suspect they would lose the best part. I am forty, I live in a caravan and I have no pension. Is it betrayal to choose security?
What do you recommend to Róisín?
Accept and use the pool as a first step before taking students to the sea.
She designs a course that always ends at Inch. Her friends criticise her, but many students reach the sea.
Refuse and look for public funding for her beach school.
She gets a small grant from the county. It isn’t much, but it gets her through the winter.
Accept only a one-year contract to try it out.
At the end of the year she has saved quite a lot and goes back to the beach with a new van.
The project needs a lot of water and energy, and a report says it would use as much as a village of three thousand people. The company promises to use wind energy. Does that change your answer?
Is it betrayal to change your ideals for security?
No, because we all need… / Sometimes yes, when…
Have you done it?
Do you regret it?
Can the artificial replace the natural?
In some cases yes, for example… / Never completely because…
What example do you use?
Do you prefer it?
What scares you more: having no money or having no freedom?
I’m more afraid of… because…
Have you always thought that?
And your family?
Is learning without risk really learning?
I think risk… / You can learn well without…
What did you learn with a bit of fear?
Do you recommend it?

It is early. Orla is in the ice-cream shop’s kitchen. She makes ice cream with milk from Kerry cows, seaweed from the beach and gin from a local distillery. On the wall there is a photo of a dolphin.

That is Fungie, the harbour dolphin. He lived here for thirty-seven years, alone, and played with the boats. The whole town lived off him: boats, T-shirts, cuddly toys. In 2020 he disappeared. I made a blue ice cream in his honour. Is there a famous animal in your city?

It is St Stephen’s Day, the twenty-sixth of December. The “wren boys” parade through the streets of Dingle: groups with straw masks, drums and colourful costumes. Orla closes the ice-cream shop and goes out with her band. Before that she tells you this festival almost disappeared when she was a child.

When I was little, only a few old men went out and we children were scared of the masks. In the nineties there was hardly anyone left. Then a group of young people revived it and now thousands of people come. I love it, but sometimes it feels more like a show for tourists than our own festival. I put on a mask and play.

I prefer to watch and film a video.

The council wants to charge tourists an entrance fee to see the parade and so pay for the cleaning. Orla doesn’t know what to think. What do you think?

Dingle is filling up with holiday rentals. In summer there are more beds for visitors than for residents. Orla has two young employees who can’t find anywhere to live and are sleeping in a van. She has a flat above the shop that she could rent to tourists for a lot of money or to her employees for very little.

With what I earn renting the flat in July and August I pay the mortgage for the whole year. If I give it to my employees, I have to raise the price of the ice cream or let someone go in winter. If I don’t, they will leave for Tralee and I will lose my team. The whole town says the problem is holiday rentals, but almost all of us have one. Who should change first?
What do you recommend to Orla?
Rent the flat to her employees and explain to customers why the ice cream costs more.
She puts a sign on the door. Many customers leave extra tips; some complain.
Rent it to tourists in summer and to her employees the rest of the year.
The employees accept, but in summer they have to go back to the van.
Organise the shop owners to demand a limit on holiday rentals.
The meeting is tense: many live off those rentals. But they agree to look into it.
One of her employees confesses that, if he gets the cheap flat, he plans to sublet a room to tourists to save money. Does that change Orla’s decision?

Yes, especially rents… / Not much, because…

Would it work?
